A road through the park leads toward the Pacific coast. Short stops offer views of lakes and mountain valleys, while longer routes let visitors explore the highland landscape on foot. The weather changes quickly, and the altitude can be felt even on short walks.

Calakmul was an influential Maya city and a political rival of Tikal. Its buildings stand amid the forests of Campeche. Large pyramids and the remains of urban development give a sense of the settlement's size and the role monumental structures played in its life.

Structures I and II are among its best-known buildings. A visit brings archaeology and tropical forest together: ancient stone buildings stand among dense vegetation. Calakmul adds to an exploration of other Maya cities by offering the chance to see a large complex in a natural setting, far from a modern city center.

In Calderón, one of the most interesting places to linger is a craftsperson's workbench. This district in northern Quito preserves the tradition of making figurines known locally as mazapán. Small characters, flowers and animals take shape from a flour-based dough, while delicate painting adds detail. These are decorative objects; the name belongs to the local craft tradition.

The work unfolds in several stages. First, the craftsperson shapes the material, then begins decorating it. This is where patience and precision become particularly clear: a tiny brushstroke turns into a pattern on clothing, while a few colors bring a miniature to life. Behind every finished souvenir lie skills passed down through families and workshops.

A visit to Calderón makes a journey through Quito's surroundings more rewarding. Here you can discover the craft and choose a small handmade keepsake; access to a particular workshop is confirmed when the itinerary is arranged. The stop will appeal to travelers who enjoy talking with local artisans and bringing home objects with a story they understand.

Caleta Tortel is a small coastal settlement in the Aysén Region of Chilean Patagonia. It sits amid water, steep forested slopes and damp southern forests, not far from the mouth of the Baker River. Instead of walking along conventional streets, visitors follow wooden paths, stairways and boardwalks linking houses along the shore.

This layout shapes the experience of visiting: the bay is always close, and the walkways reveal new views of wooden houses and forest. On cruise itineraries, going ashore and exploring on foot depend on the weather and conditions for approaching the coast. Comfortable shoes and clothing suited to Patagonia's rainy climate are useful for a visit to Tortel.
